sentences: On a long, low canvas, a sphinx with a woman's face and a leopard's body leans her cheek against a young man.
The canvas is three times as wide as it is tall, stretching the moment out like a dream.
Nothing moves, and yet the air is charged.
The painter is the Belgian Symbolist Fernand Khnopff.
In 1883 he helped found Les XX, a Brussels circle of avant-garde artists, and this is often called his most famous painting.
Khnopff reworked Gustave Moreau's Oedipus and the Sphinx of 1864 in his own language.
Moreau's sphinx clings to the hero as she confronts him; this one simply leans in, quiet and close.
Look at the sphinx's face.
Eyes half shut and a faint smile on her lips, she presses her cheek to his.
Some read this face as the painter's sister Marguerite, his favourite model.
The two touching faces could not be more different.
He stares straight ahead without any expression at all, lips closed and gaze fixed, as if refusing to be moved by her touch.
Some see the painter himself in this Oedipus-like youth.
His slender, smooth body makes it hard to tell whether this is a man or a woman.
In his hand is a staff topped with wings and a blue orb.
Khnopff was known for exactly this kind of androgynous figure.
Now follow the sphinx's body.
Her spotted leopard body stretches far to the right.
One paw curls around the young man's waist, and her long tail, banded with dark rings, reaches almost to the right-hand edge.
In the background stand slender blue columns and a wall of mock hieroglyphs, with a reddish plain stretching away beyond them.
They make the scene feel like a temple in a dream rather than any real place.
Nothing here belongs to a particular time or country.
Khnopff left almost no visible brushstrokes, painting with a cool, smooth finish.
Chilly blues, warm flesh and tawny fur play against each other, calm on the surface but taut underneath.
That smoothness makes the scene feel even less real, like an image seen in a dream.
The painting is also known as Art.
It leaves the old fin-de-siècle tension between seduction and control, ideal and desire, as an unsolved riddle.
His work went on to influence Gustav Klimt and the artists of the Vienna Secession.
Step back and look again.
Who is tempting whom here, and who is holding out?
Of the two faces touching, ask yourself which one is hiding more.
There may be no right answer, and that is part of the spell.
